title: How to Break a Child's Spirit in 24 Pages
author: Roger McFillin
summary: Psychologist Roger McFillin critiques My Life with Anxiety, a picture book for seven-year-olds in which a cheerleader copes with nerves by chewing half a CBD gummy and having friends come to her house. He makes clear his target is not the child but the adults who wrote, edited, published, and shelved the book, arguing they have caught an ideology that equates love with sparing children every discomfort. McFillin extends the book's logic satirically to imagined sequels on butterflies, boredom, and grief, then lists the false lessons it teaches: that anxiety is a dangerous condition, that avoidance is the remedy, and that relief comes from something swallowed. He argues anxiety is the body preparing for something that matters, that avoidance makes fear grow while life shrinks, and that the habit of numbing outlasts the candy. His conclusion is that such books teach children to surrender the capacity to feel something hard and come out stronger.
points: The book presents a nervous stomach before cheer practice as a condition managed with half a CBD gummy.
McFillin argues that labeling ordinary nervousness as a disorder sets children apart from their peers for life.
Avoiding feared situations, he says, is the most reliable way to make the fear grow.
He warns that a gummy at seven can become a diagnosis at ten and a prescription by fourteen.
The core capacity at stake is the ability to feel something hard, stay with it, and grow from it.
quotes: I want to be clear about who this piece is aimed at before I go any further. The girl in this book is a real child, and she is not my target. The adults are.
The adults around her caught an ideology, one that feeds on our empathy and hands us back a lie: that to love a child is to spare her every discomfort. That isn't love. It's surrender.

In the span of a single page, a child learns that anxiety is dangerous, that it lives inside her as a condition setting her apart from other kids, and that like a peanut allergy it has to be managed for the rest of her life.

Each avoided sleepover teaches a child a little more convincingly that the world is dangerous and that she is not equipped to handle it, so her fear gets bigger while her life gets smaller, and the adults around her call this a disorder.
Tomorrow it's a pill, then a drink, then a prescription, because the habit outlasts the candy. This book isn't teaching her to cope. It's teaching her to numb.

Books like this do not protect children. They teach them to surrender the most important capacity a human being has, which is the ability to feel something hard, stay with it, and come out the other side stronger for it.
